headline: It looks like a good time to plan a conversation
whatWeNoticed: Your answers point to some real changes worth attention. This isn't an emergency — it's a signal that it's time to talk and start planning together.
whatDeservesAttentionFirst: The changes you noticed in safety and day-to-day routines deserve attention first, because small adjustments now can prevent a crisis later.
helpfulObservationsToMonitor: Any new stumbles, dizziness, or changes in walking
Whether daily tasks (meals, medications, bills) are slipping
Changes in mood, energy, or withdrawing from others
todayThisWeek: Write down the specific things you've noticed, with dates.
Schedule a check-in visit with your parent's doctor.
Have one gentle, low-pressure conversation with your parent.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Waiting for a crisis before acting — early is easier for everyone.
Taking over decisions instead of involving your parent.
Trying to fix everything in one conversation.
Not writing down what you observe before the doctor's visit.

withYourParent: Pick a calm, unhurried moment — not right after a scare.
Lead with love and concern, not logistics: 'I've noticed… and I care about you.'
Ask questions and listen; let them keep as much control as possible.
withFamily: Get siblings on the same page before approaching your parent.
Agree on who does what, so no one person carries it all.
Share what each person has observed — patterns become clearer together.

questionsForHealthcareTeam: Could any medications be affecting balance, memory, or mood?
Is a falls-risk or memory assessment appropriate now?
What changes should prompt us to call you sooner?
whatMayBeComingNext: If changes continue, a more complete assessment can clarify priorities.
Planning ahead now (safety, support, documents) makes future decisions calmer.
howToPrepare: Start a simple observation journal to track changes over time.
Locate key documents (medications list, insurance, any advance directives).
whatThisDoesNotMean: This does not mean your parent has dementia or must move.
It does not mean you've done anything wrong — noticing early is a strength.
suggestedNextSteps: Take the full Comprehensive Assessment (coming soon) for a complete picture.
